summary: Provides the External Data Representation (XDR) description of the NFS version 4 protocol. It lists the data structures and operations in a machine-readable form, separate from the main protocol specification in RFC 7530.

eli5.summary: The main NFS document is the rulebook, and this one is the exact list of forms and boxes used in every message, written so computers can read it.

questions: how to extract nfs4_prot.x from rfc 7531
what is the nfsv4 program number
subtitle: The machine-readable XDR file that defines every data structure and operation on the wire in NFS version 4.0.

tldr.problem: The NFSv4.0 protocol needs an exact, compilable description of every request, reply and data type so that independent implementations encode them identically.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC embeds the full External Data Representation (XDR) description of NFSv4.0 in its text, with a sentinel prefix on each line and a one-line shell script that extracts it into a ready-to-compile file.
tldr.outcome: Together with RFC 7530 it replaces RFC 3530 as the definition of NFS version 4. It contains no prose rules of its own and defers security to RFC 7530.

today: RFC 7531 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2015, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is the XDR companion to RFC 7530, and the abstract says the two together replace RFC 3530.

sections.title: What This Document Is
sections.content:
This document contains the External Data Representation (XDR) description of the NFSv4.0 protocol that RFC 7530 specifies. XDR itself is defined in RFC 4506. The abstract recalls that NFS version 4 descends from versions 2 (RFC 1094) and 3 (RFC 1813), and adds file locking and the MOUNT protocol into one protocol, plus strong security with negotiation, COMPOUND operations, client caching and internationalization.

The abstract also states that RFC 7530 formally obsoletes RFC 3530, and that this document, together with RFC 7530, replaces RFC 3530 as the definition of the NFS version 4 protocol.
sections.eli5: This is the blueprint that shows the exact shape of every message NFS can send, while the other document explains what the messages mean.

sections.title: Extracting the .x File
sections.content:
The XDR description is laid out so a reader can extract it in compile-ready form. Every line of the description starts with the sentinel ///. Feeding the document to a short shell script removes the leading white space and the sentinel, leaving the machine-readable file.

If the script is saved as extract.sh and the document as spec.txt, the command sh extract.sh < spec.txt > nfs4_prot.x produces the file. The text of the RFC includes the license header for the code and notes that the file was derived from RFC 7531.
sections.eli5: The special marks at the start of each line are like highlighter. A tiny program picks out only the highlighted lines and makes a clean copy for computers.

sections.title: Basic Types, Sizes and File Types
sections.content:
The file starts with size constants: NFS4_FHSIZE is 128, NFS4_VERIFIER_SIZE is 8, NFS4_OTHER_SIZE is 12 and NFS4_OPAQUE_LIMIT is 1024. It also names the maximum values of 32-bit and 64-bit integers.

The enum nfs_ftype4 lists the object types: regular file (1), directory (2), block device (3), character device (4), symbolic link (5), socket (6), fifo (7), attribute directory (8) and named attribute (9).

A set of basic typedefs follows, such as offset4, length4, clientid4, changeid4, a filehandle nfs_fh4 of at most NFS4_FHSIZE bytes, and several UTF-8 string types. Time is a structure nfstime4 with a 64-bit seconds and a 32-bit nseconds. Other structures cover stateid4 (a 32-bit seqid plus an other field of NFS4_OTHER_SIZE bytes), client IDs and lock owners.
sections.eli5: Before building anything, the file lists the basic building blocks: how big a number can be, what kinds of files exist, and how a time is written down.

sections.title: Status Codes
sections.content:
The enum nfsstat4 defines the result status of every operation. NFS4_OK is 0. Values from the older NFS family keep their small numbers, for example NFS4ERR_PERM is 1, NFS4ERR_NOENT is 2 and NFS4ERR_ACCESS is 13. Codes specific to NFSv4 start at 10001 with NFS4ERR_BADHANDLE and run up to 10048, NFS4ERR_CB_PATH_DOWN.

Many of the NFSv4 codes concern state: NFS4ERR_STALE_CLIENTID, NFS4ERR_STALE_STATEID, NFS4ERR_OLD_STATEID, NFS4ERR_BAD_STATEID and NFS4ERR_BAD_SEQID, together with lock and grace-period errors such as NFS4ERR_DENIED, NFS4ERR_EXPIRED and NFS4ERR_GRACE. NFS4ERR_WRONGSEC reports the wrong security flavor and NFS4ERR_BADXDR reports that XDR decoding failed.
sections.eli5: Every answer comes with a number that says how it went. Zero means fine, and the other numbers each name a different kind of problem.

sections.title: File Attributes and Access Control
sections.content:
File attributes are described by numbered constants and matching typedefs. The mandatory attributes are numbered 0 to 11 plus FATTR4_FILEHANDLE as 19, starting with FATTR4_SUPPORTED_ATTRS (0), FATTR4_TYPE (1) and FATTR4_SIZE (4). Recommended attributes run through 55 (FATTR4_MOUNTED_ON_FILEID) and include FATTR4_ACL (12), FATTR4_MODE (33), FATTR4_OWNER (36) and the time attributes.

A set of attributes travels in the fattr4 structure: a bitmap, attrmask, saying which attributes are present, and an opaque list, attr_vals, holding their values.

Access control uses nfsace4, an entry with a type, flag, access_mask and who. The ACE types are allow (0), deny (1), audit (2) and alarm (3). The file also defines inheritance flags, the access mask bits such as ACE4_READ_DATA and ACE4_WRITE_ACL, combined values such as ACE4_GENERIC_READ (0x00120081), and the permission bits for the mode attribute such as MODE4_RUSR and MODE4_SUID.
sections.eli5: Every file has a little card of facts, such as its size, owner and who may read it. Each fact has a number so one message can say which facts it wants.

sections.title: Operations and the COMPOUND Procedure
sections.content:
Each operation has an arguments structure and a result. Results are mostly unions switched on nfsstat4: on NFS4_OK they carry the success data, and otherwise they are void. A few, such as LOCK4res, also carry data for a specific error like NFS4ERR_DENIED. Comments in the arguments note which filehandle the operation acts on, for example CURRENT_FH or SAVED_FH.

The enum nfs_opnum4 numbers the operations from OP_ACCESS (3) to OP_RELEASE_LOCKOWNER (39), with OP_ILLEGAL at 10044. They include OP_OPEN (18), OP_READ (25), OP_WRITE (38), OP_LOCK (12), OP_GETATTR (9) and OP_SETCLIENTID (35). The OPEN arguments can ask for read, write or both share access, name a claim type, and the result may include an open delegation of type none, read or write.

The remote program NFS4_PROGRAM is number 100003 at version 4 and has only two procedures. NFSPROC4_NULL is procedure 0. NFSPROC4_COMPOUND is procedure 1 and carries a COMPOUND4args with a tag, a minorversion and an array of operations, argarray. The reply holds an overall status, the tag and an array of results.
sections.eli5: NFS has only two real doors: one that does nothing and one that takes a whole to-do list. Each item on the list is a job like open, read or write, and the answer comes back as a matching list.

sections.title: Callbacks from Server to Client
sections.content:
The file also defines a second program, NFS4_CALLBACK, that lets the server call the client. Its program number is 0x40000000, in the transient range, because the client assigns the exact number and gives it to the server through SETCLIENTID. Its version is 1 and it has CB_NULL (0) and CB_COMPOUND (1).

Only two callback operations are defined: OP_CB_GETATTR (3) and OP_CB_RECALL (4), plus OP_CB_ILLEGAL for invalid operation numbers. CB_RECALL4args carries a stateid, a truncate flag and a filehandle. CB_COMPOUND4args adds a callback_ident field to the tag and minor version.
sections.eli5: Usually the client calls the server, but sometimes the server needs to call back, for example to ask for a borrowed file to be returned.

sections.title: Security
sections.content: This document adds no security text of its own. Its Security Considerations section says only to see the Security Considerations section of RFC 7530. The only normative references are RFC 4506 for XDR and RFC 7530 for the protocol.
sections.eli5: This document only holds the blueprint, so the safety rules are all in the main rulebook, RFC 7530.
